summary:
Dmitry Buykin of Maersk delivers a practitioner report on deploying AI agents in global shipping operations. He frames the central challenge as 'tribal dungeons': operational knowledge exists inside organizations but is captured as legacy SOPs—screenshots showing what a person sees and where they click. These are intelligible to humans but useless to an agent, which instead needs preconditions, decisions, identifiers, backend calls, validation, recovery, and evidence of successful execution. Translating this tacit knowledge, negotiated between experts (who own the 'what') and agents (who own the 'how'), consumed most of the project.

Buykin argues that the agent loop itself is not the system; the refining loop around it is. The corpus of procedures outweighs the runtime roughly twenty to one, because the same shipping step means different things in different countries. In production, over 200 agent instances run concurrently against legacy backends, with execution times ranging from minutes to ten minutes.

Quality, he says, was not designed upfront but earned through more than 100,000 corrections over nine months. Heat maps of traces turn thousands of failure scenarios into priorities, with a single red cell often costing the team a month or two of work. A correction only counts once it becomes an executable change—the line between an opinion and a production fix. He distinguishes discovery (needing agent freedom) from production (needing a cage), insisting that 'please be careful' is not a guardrail. The resulting methodology rests on five moves: make work representable, execution bounded, behavior observable, correction cheap, and improvement compounding, delivered via composite tools rolled out across countries in one go.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The long tail is the expensive part
sections.summary: Frames the talk as a practitioner report on the hard part most agent demos skip: turning messy operational knowledge into something an agent can execute safely. The easy majority is automated; what remains is the long tail of exceptions, including cases requiring expert orchestration across multiple incomplete legacy systems.

sections.title: What an SOP has to become for an agent
sections.summary: Introduces 'tribal dungeons': knowledge exists in legacy SOPs as screenshots of what a person sees and clicks, which is unusable by agents. An agent SOP needs preconditions, decisions, identifiers, backend calls, validation, recovery, and evidence. Translation between experts (who own the what) and agents (who own the how) is most of the effort.

sections.title: The refining loop is the system
sections.summary: Describes a three-part architecture: SOP memory corpus, execution runtime, and feedback capture. The agent loop is not the system; the refining loop around it is. The procedure corpus is roughly twenty times larger than the runtime, because the same step means different things across countries.

sections.title: Running 200 instances against legacy backends
sections.summary: Reports over 200 concurrent instances in production, with latencies ranging from a few minutes to up to ten minutes. The main reason is dependency on slow legacy systems that cannot be faster than the agent loop itself.

sections.title: Triage, traces, and shared evidence
sections.summary: Explains that expert time is the bottleneck, so triage is automated by clustering failures and handing back actionable items. The trace is shared evidence that lets experts and engineers review the same case and agree on what happened. A correction only counts when it becomes an executable change.

sections.title: Where vibe coding and spec driven work run out
sections.summary: Argues quality comes from replaying real examples with disabled writes to protect production, not from vibes or bigger models. Vibe coding and spec-driven development typically cannot improve accuracy beyond early stages at this scale; the real work starts with applied engineering common sense.

sections.title: A hundred thousand corrections, and heat maps
sections.summary: States that accuracy was earned incrementally, not designed upfront. Over 100,000 corrections were made over nine months. Heat maps turn thousands of traces into priorities that align experts and engineers. Turning one red cell typically costs the full team one to two months of work.

sections.title: Please be careful is not a guardrail
sections.summary: Contrasts discovery (which needs agent freedom) with production (which needs a cage). The harness exists to make dumb mistakes impossible, not to give the model more room. Critical paths keep review and approval in the loop; engineering focuses on safe hand-offs and a trustworthy trail.

sections.title: Five moves, and compounding improvement
sections.summary: Summarizes the methodology in five moves: make work representable, execution bounded, behavior observable, corrections cheap, and improvement compound. AI-native operation folds what works back into code as composite tools adapting to applications and people.

sections.title: Composite tools, and why they skip MCP
sections.summary: Describes aggregating repeatable successful sequences into larger tools that combine proven scenarios as reusable snippets for other agents, rollable out to hundreds of countries at once. Concludes by explaining why MCPs are not used: legacy systems are bloated, and direct function-calling wrappers let them distill responses and control quality.

limitations: Vibe coding and spec-driven development cannot reliably improve accuracy beyond early stages at this scale
'Please be careful' is explicitly described as not a guardrail
Agent speed is bottlenecked by legacy backend latency
MCPs are described as not the best choice for their bloated legacy systems
